title: Post-Course Portfolio: Project Management App
descriptionMarkdown:
# Project Management App

## Position in the curriculum

Post-course portfolio: build after finishing the full curriculum through the final capstone, and after the Authentication & User Management System, whose role-based authorization this project extends into a genuinely per-resource permission model (permission depends on team membership, not just a global role).

## What is graded, and what is external

This project has a dedicated, automatically-graded checkpoint: **`role-gated-task-checkpoint`** ("Role-gated task board"), a pure in-memory `TaskBoard.run(String input)` program implementing exactly the team/membership/task/per-resource-authorization core, including the rule that a task's current assignee may always reassign it themselves even without being a team owner. Passing its hidden tests proves this authorization logic is correct.

The real event publication and notification persistence are external and self-reviewed, since the sandbox cannot verify an asynchronous side effect landing in a real database.

## Architecture overview

```text
TeamController / TaskController
TaskBoardService                 <- your checkpoint's authorization rules, reshaped as a Spring bean
Team / Membership (JPA entities)  <- membership carries a role: OWNER or MEMBER
Task (JPA entity)                  <- team, assignee, status, dueDate
TaskCompletedEvent / TaskOverdueEvent  <- Spring application events
NotificationListener               <- @EventListener, persists a Notification row, decoupled from TaskBoardService
```

## Build it as vertical slices

1. **Slice 1 — port the checkpoint logic into a service.** Carry your team/membership/task/authorization rules into `TaskBoardService`, unit tests unchanged.
2. **Slice 2 — persistence.** JPA entities for `Team`, `Membership`, `Task`; the authorization checks now query real membership rows instead of an in-memory map.
3. **Slice 3 — domain events on completion.** Publish a `TaskCompletedEvent` when a task's status changes to done; a separate `NotificationListener` (a different class, tested independently) turns it into a persisted `Notification` row.
4. **Slice 4 — overdue detection.** A scheduled check (or an on-demand query) using an injected `Clock` flags tasks past their due date and publishes an event for each, exactly once.
5. **Slice 5 — the full authorization matrix, end to end.** Every role/operation combination from your checkpoint's tests, now exercised through real HTTP requests with real authenticated users.

## Common pitfalls

- **Letting the task-update code directly call the notification component.** This couples two things that should be independent; publish an event and let a listener react, so `TaskBoardService` never needs to know notifications exist at all.
- **Checking global role instead of per-team membership.** A user who owns Team A is not automatically an owner of Team B; every check must be scoped to the specific team a task belongs to, exactly as your checkpoint's tests require.
- **Reading the system clock directly in the overdue check**, making it untestable without waiting for real time; inject a `Clock`.
- **Generating a duplicate notification every time the overdue check runs**, instead of only once per newly-overdue task. Track what has already been notified.

## How to self-test what the checkpoint cannot reach

- Publish a `TaskCompletedEvent` in a unit test with no real database and confirm the listener alone correctly builds the expected `Notification`, without needing the rest of the application running.
- Advance an injected clock past a task's due date, run the overdue check, and confirm exactly one notification is created — then run the check again and confirm no duplicate is created.
- As a `MEMBER` of Team A, attempt an `OWNER`-only action on a Team B resource you also happen to be a `MEMBER` of, and confirm the per-team (not global) authorization check rejects it correctly if you are not an owner of that specific team.

## Required evidence

- An authorization test matrix covering every role and every protected operation, including a `MEMBER` attempting an `OWNER`-only action.
- A test confirming a task update publishes exactly the expected event, and a separate test confirming the notification listener correctly turns that event into a stored notification, with the two components tested independently.
- A test for the overdue-task detection using an injected `Clock`, not the system clock.
- A migration history showing the team/membership schema introduced and later extended (for example, adding a new role) as two separate, ordered migrations.
- A short architecture note explaining why the notification listener depends on the task service's published event type rather than the task service depending on the notification component directly.

## Review and completion

A reviewer joins a new member to a team as a `MEMBER`, attempts an `OWNER`-only action as that member (expecting rejection), then performs the same action as the actual `OWNER` (expecting success), and finally advances the system clock past a task's due date and confirms exactly one notification is generated for the right user, not zero and not duplicated on a later, unrelated request.
learningObjectives: Complete the graded role-gated task board checkpoint and carry its verified per-team authorization rules into a real JPA-backed service
Design and test a role-based, per-resource authorization model with more than one permission level
Publish a domain event on a state change and handle it in a component the publisher does not depend on
Detect a time-based condition (an overdue task) deterministically with an injected clock, without duplicating a notification
Evolve a schema through separate, ordered migrations as requirements grow
